title: Autumn at Astor
kicker: Ghost stories · October customs · November fires
deck: Sleepy Hollow, ghost-story collections and the history of Bonfire Night: reading for the weeks when the evenings draw in.
intro: Autumn’s shelf begins with stories that suit an evening’s reading: Irving’s Headless Horseman, American and Victorian ghost fiction, and the investigations of Carnacki. Longer supernatural tales take the reader from the Danube to a remote Irish house.

The books come from the American, Victorian and Modern Classics collections. The Halloween collection explains how older stories came to be linked with October, and A Victorian Bonfire Night follows the changing customs of the Fifth of November. Both draw on historical sources.

sections.title: Ghost stories for an autumn evening
sections.description: Pick a single story from a collection, or read one writer through a whole volume. There are American stories, Victorian ghosts, M. R. James’s antiquarian tales and Carnacki’s investigations.

sections.title: Strange places and uncertain witnesses
sections.description: Rivers, forests, country houses and isolated rooms give these stories their settings.

sections.title: October into November
sections.description: Read about the Fifth of November through Victorian fiction, folklore and contemporary reporting, then continue with longer Gothic fiction for the dark evenings.

readingNote.title: A practical autumn reading sequence
paragraphs: For a short first session, use the Sleepy Hollow close reading alongside Irving’s story. Follow it with one tale from American Ghost Stories or M. R. James. That way you can put several kinds of supernatural writing side by side without taking on a novel a week.

Move to A Victorian Bonfire Night around 5 November, or use it at any time as a source-based history of the festival. Its regional examples, newspaper material and accounts of food, fireworks and policing explain why the holiday was never observed in one uniform way.

title: Halloween at Astor
deck: Headless horsemen, haunted houses, vampires and uncanny landscapes, with the books and guides that explain their literary history.
intro: Start with Sleepy Hollow and Other American Halloween Stories: twelve complete stories whose later seasonal associations are explained alongside their original publication histories. Add Victorian and American anthologies, the ghost stories of M. R. James and E. F. Benson, Poe’s tales and Hodgson’s Carnacki investigations.

The longer-reading shelves include Dracula, Carmilla, Frankenstein and works in which the evidence of a haunting remains contested. The free guides below cover Halloween’s literary history, ghost stories, Gothic fiction and individual works. Close readings offer shorter starting points for a class, reading group or evening at home.

siteTheme.ribbonNote: Ghost stories, Gothic novels and the history of 31 October

sections.title: The Halloween story shelf
sections.description: Anthologies and author collections make it possible to choose one complete story for a reading session. The dedicated Halloween anthology also traces how familiar October imagery became attached to earlier literature.

sections.title: Haunted rooms, rivers and forests
sections.description: Novellas and short fiction with close attention to place, testimony and the limits of explanation. The Blackwood and Hodgson editions include publication history and researched context.

sections.title: Gothic novels and transformations
sections.description: Two vampire stories, a scientific creation, a divided identity and a supernatural portrait give five ways into Gothic fiction. Wuthering Heights adds a ghost bound up with family history and with competing narrators.

sections.title: Supernatural drama and verse
sections.description: For a change of form, read Marlowe’s drama of a pact with the devil or Coleridge’s narrative poem of an extraordinary voyage. These are selections for supernatural reading, each with its own literary and religious context.

readingNote.title: How a story becomes a Halloween story
paragraphs: The twelve works in Sleepy Hollow and Other American Halloween Stories were not originally written for Halloween. Their later association with the festival grew through the repeated use of ghosts, witches, black cats, haunted houses and other supernatural figures in American October culture.

Keeping those two histories separate makes the reading more useful. First ask when and where a story appeared, who narrates it and what evidence it gives. Then consider the customs, adaptations and later publications through which it became familiar seasonal reading.

title: Bonfire Night at Astor
deck: The Fifth of November in fiction, newspapers and popular custom, with Shakespeare’s early Stuart world alongside it.
intro: This short collection is built round A Victorian Bonfire Night, which prints nineteenth-century fiction, essays, folklore and reporting with new historical chapters on the Plot, its commemoration, bonfire societies, food, fireworks and policing.
Macbeth is here because it was written soon after the Gunpowder Plot and shares its concerns with kingship, treason and equivocation, although the play is set in medieval Scotland.

sections.title: The history of the Fifth
sections.description: The dedicated anthology follows the festival through Victorian writing and documented local customs.

sections.title: Shakespeare and the early Stuart context
sections.description: Macbeth has a royal murder, a disputed succession and a porter who jokes about an equivocator. Choose the annotated play or the expanded scholarly edition; the guides below cover its text and history.

readingNote.title: From the Plot to the annual observance
paragraphs: The Gunpowder Plot attempted to destroy Parliament and kill James I at the opening planned for 5 November 1605. Its discovery was followed by an annual religious commemoration established by Parliament in 1606. UK Parliament’s historical account records the services and sermons that made the date a recurring public observance.

The Astor anthology follows how the celebration changed after 1605. It covers the repeal of the statutory observance in 1859, local bonfire societies, commercial fireworks, fuel gathering, disturbances and seasonal food. Anti-Catholic hostility is part of that history too.

sources.label: UK Parliament: commemoration of the Gunpowder Plot

title: Christmas at Astor
kicker: Christmas books · Winter customs · Twelfth Night
deck: Dickens, American Christmas stories, the history of familiar traditions and ghost stories for the fireside.
intro: The Christmas collection brings together the dedicated seasonal books in the Astor catalogue: four individual Dickens Christmas books, their collected edition, American Christmas Stories and the cultural history A Victorian Christmas.

Two older Christmas entertainments, the ghost story told by the fire and the festive comedy, have shelves of their own. There are also free guides on Dickens, Christmas traditions and supernatural fiction, close readings, and the study edition of A Christmas Carol.

sections.title: Christmas collections and customs
sections.description: Dickens at Christmas has four of his Christmas books in one volume. American Christmas Stories has eight stories and a poem, and A Victorian Christmas is a history of trees, cards, crackers, food, work, charity and Christmas publishing.

sections.title: Dickens’s Christmas books
sections.description: Each is published in its own volume, with its own notes. The Chimes is set on New Year’s Eve, and in The Haunted Man a chemist is offered the power to forget his sorrows.

sections.title: Ghost stories by the fire
sections.description: The Turn of the Screw opens with ghost stories told round the fire on Christmas Eve. M. R. James read his own stories to friends at Christmas, and Victorian Ghost Stories collects the tradition both belong to.

sections.title: Christmas chapters in longer novels
sections.description: Great Expectations opens with Pip on the marshes on Christmas Eve and at the family Christmas dinner. In The Wind in the Willows, field-mice come carol-singing to Mole’s house and stay for supper, in the chapter ‘Dulce Domum’.

sections.title: The close of the Christmas season
sections.description: Twelfth Night is named after the last night of the Christmas season and is full of disguise, music and household disorder. Its first recorded performance was in February 1602.

readingNote.title: Christmas traditions have histories
paragraphs: A Victorian Christmas explains familiar objects and customs through changes in postage, transport, publishing, commerce and household work, and looks back to practices older than Victoria’s reign. A tree, a card, a carol and a Christmas dinner each have a history of their own.

Dickens at Christmas contains four of the five short Christmas books Dickens published between 1843 and 1848. American Christmas Stories contains eight stories and a poem dated 1823–1905, with publication histories and historical chapters.

title: Winter at Astor
deck: New England snow, the Klondike, the Wild Wood and Shakespeare’s winter storytelling, with reading for the long evenings.
intro: These books make winter weather, northern travel or the winter household part of their subject. Ethan Frome places its central story in snowbound New England; Jack London’s novels follow working animals through the northern gold-rush world; Frankenstein begins and ends within an Arctic expedition.

A second shelf has shorter readings about rooms, firesides and remembered homes, among them Grahame’s Wild Wood and Mole’s return, Coleridge’s Frost at Midnight and the winter’s tale Mamillius begins to tell in Shakespeare’s late play.

sections.title: Snow, work and northern travel
sections.description: In these books the cold decides how far people can travel and whether they survive. Wharton writes about debt and narrow choices in a New England winter, London about animals working in the northern snow, and Shelley frames Frankenstein with an Arctic voyage.

sections.title: The winter room and the return home
sections.description: Read the Wild Wood and homecoming chapters in Grahame, Frost at Midnight among Coleridge’s selected poems, or the winter’s tale Mamillius begins to tell in Shakespeare’s play.

sections.title: At the turn of the year
sections.description: The Chimes follows Trotty Veck through New Year’s Eve. Twelfth Night, named after the last night of Christmas, is a comedy of desire and mistaken identity.

readingNote.title: Follow the season in the text
paragraphs: For a winter reading group, compare what cold weather requires people or animals to do. Transport, food, shelter, work and money are concrete concerns in Ethan Frome and the London novels. Frankenstein uses the Arctic expedition to frame another narrator’s history and to place Walton’s ambition beside Victor’s.

The Winter’s Tale should be read with its changing seasons in view. The play moves from the danger surrounding Leontes’s household to the pastoral scenes after a sixteen-year interval. Its title does not mean the whole action occurs in winter; the contrast between winter storytelling and the later festival is part of the reading.

title: Spring at Astor
deck: The Mole’s spring-cleaning, Wordsworth’s first mild day of March, the spring song that ends Love’s Labour’s Lost and Tess walking to Talbothays on a May morning.
intro: Spring in these books is usually a particular day. The Mole abandons his spring-cleaning for the river bank; Wordsworth writes to his sister on the first mild day of March; Anne of Green Gables lives through a reluctant Canadian spring; Tess sets out for Talbothays on a thyme-scented May morning; Elizabeth Bennet is at Hunsford, a short walk from Rosings, over Easter.

The poems and plays use the season as a convention to play with. Shakespeare ends Love’s Labour’s Lost with a song for spring and another for winter; Blake’s ‘Spring’ belongs to Songs of Innocence; Milton’s Eden has a perpetual spring that the Fall brings to an end. Each edition below is listed with its guides and close readings.

sections.title: The season in the novels
sections.description: Grahame opens with the Mole’s spring-cleaning, Montgomery gives a chapter to the Canadian spring, Hardy sends Tess to the dairy in May and Austen brings Darcy to Rosings for Easter. Werther’s first letter is dated 4 May.

sections.title: Spring in poetry
sections.description: Wordsworth’s ‘Lines Written in Early Spring’ and ‘To My Sister’, Blake’s ‘Spring’ and ‘The Echoing Green’, Shakespeare’s sonnet of absence in spring, and the perpetual spring of Milton’s Eden.

sections.title: Shakespeare in spring
sections.description: The spring song that closes Love’s Labour’s Lost, the pages’ song of a lover and his lass in As You Like It, Perdita’s daffodils in The Winter’s Tale and the rite of May in A Midsummer Night’s Dream.

readingNote.title: Two springs side by side
paragraphs: Read Wordsworth’s ‘Lines Written in Early Spring’ beside Blake’s ‘Spring’. Wordsworth sits in a grove and ends with a complaint about what man has made of man; Blake gives it to a child and a lamb and leaves the argument out.

For a longer route, follow the Mole out of his burrow in the first chapter of The Wind in the Willows, then read the Talbothays chapters of Tess, where the spring and summer at the dairy are the happiest stretch of her life.

shelf.label: Blake’s ‘Spring’
shelf.title: Songs of Innocence and of Experience

title: Summer at Astor
deck: Boats on the Thames, the riverbank, summer resorts and outdoor Shakespeare: a shelf for long days and holiday reading.
intro: These books are set in summer places: a Thames boating holiday, the riverbank in The Wind in the Willows, children out of doors, lakes and gardens. Several novels follow the social life of a summer visit or a resort.

The Shakespeare shelf has a wood near Athens, the Forest of Arden and Prospero’s island, for theatre companies and reading groups. Each edition below is listed with its guides, study material and close readings.

sections.title: Rivers, railways and childhood adventures
sections.description: Start with Jerome’s comic Thames journey, Grahame’s riverbank, the children beside Nesbit’s railway or Twain’s Mississippi town.

sections.title: Summer places and social lives
sections.description: The shelf runs from Montgomery’s Canadian landscapes to the summer resort of The Awakening, the Long Island summer of The Great Gatsby and the June day of Mrs Dalloway. In all of them, leisure also involves work, money, family and social rules.

sections.title: Shakespeare outdoors
sections.description: A Midsummer Night’s Dream sends its lovers into a wood, As You Like It sends its exiles to the Forest of Arden, and The Tempest is set on Prospero’s island. The expanded Midsummer edition adds scholarly material on the same play.

readingNote.title: Choose a place, then compare it
paragraphs: A river sequence can begin with Three Men in a Boat and continue with The Wind in the Willows or Adventures of Huckleberry Finn. Compare the work of travelling, the relation between river and shore, and the narrator’s treatment of the people encountered along the way.

For a shorter group programme, read the opening of Mrs Dalloway with the summer parties in The Great Gatsby or the Grand Isle chapters of The Awakening, and compare the weather, the visits, the clothes and what each society expects.

title: Love & Valentine’s at Astor
deck: Sonnets, Shakespearean comedy and novels of courtship, with room for difficult choices as well as happy endings.
intro: These are poems, plays and novels about courtship and love. Each of Shakespeare’s sonnets can be read on its own; the comedies have mistaken identities, overheard conversations and quarrels about what lovers expect; the novels show how money and family shape a marriage.
Not every book here ends happily. The comedies and courtship novels come first; the last group is for love that ends in loss, coercion or disappointment.

sections.title: Poems and comic courtship
sections.description: Read a single sonnet, a comedy of overhearing and self-correction, or a play where disguise confuses who is pursuing whom.

sections.title: Courtship, families and social rules
sections.description: Austen’s marriages involve family income, inheritance and judgement. Montgomery and Brontë give their heroines different circumstances in which to make a choice; Wilde makes a comedy of eligibility and engagements.

sections.title: Love, loss and difficult choices
sections.description: Love affairs that end in death, separation or a slammed door.

readingNote.title: Read the relationship in its setting
paragraphs: A Valentine’s reading can be short. Sonnet 130 is a good place to start: it refuses the usual praise and still ends as a love poem. In Much Ado About Nothing, the overhearing scenes show how a character changes when presented with an account of another person’s feelings.
For the novels and later drama, follow the practical conditions of a relationship: income, inheritance, marriage law, work and the authority of relatives.

title: Fourth of July at Astor
deck: American novels, testimony and guides on liberty, slavery, community and national ambition, for reading around Independence Day.
intro: This list is for the Fourth of July and for the American writers who asked what freedom meant and who was left out of it. It starts with Frederick Douglass’s Narrative, then nineteenth-century abolitionist fiction and Twain’s novels about slavery, identity and moral judgement.
The wider shelf takes in American communities, the Civil War, work at sea and the later pursuit of wealth.

sections.title: Liberty, slavery and testimony
sections.description: Read Douglass’s first autobiography with Stowe’s abolitionist novel and Twain’s later fiction about slavery, racial classification and individual judgement. They were written decades apart, in different forms and for different purposes.

sections.title: Communities, reform and independence
sections.description: These novels are about a Puritan colony, a Mississippi childhood, a Yankee who takes nineteenth-century technology to King Arthur’s court, and a woman’s claims within marriage and social convention.

sections.title: War, work and national ambition
sections.description: Crane’s Civil War novel, Melville’s whaling voyage and Fitzgerald’s Long Island society are about war, work, wealth and the promises made about America’s future.

readingNote.title: Douglass and the national anniversary
paragraphs: On 5 July 1852, Frederick Douglass addressed an antislavery gathering in Rochester, New York. The speech now commonly known as What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July? examined the contradiction between national celebrations of liberty and the continued enslavement of people in the United States. The Library of Congress provides a historical account and links to contemporary newspaper evidence.
The Astor volume on this shelf is Douglass’s Narrative of 1845, which does not include the speech. Read it for his account of enslavement, literacy and resistance, written as abolitionist testimony.
